Artificial intelligence ( #AI ) has shown remarkable abilities to reason, problem solve, and control machines—but could tiny models of brain tissue grown in the lab do the same? Led by #BaskinEngineering Assistant Professor of Biomolecular Engineering Tal Sharf, a team of researchers at the UC Santa Cruz Genomics Institute , will explore this question with support from a $1.9 million National Science Foundation (NSF) grant. This research could drive new biomedical discoveries and lead to better therapies for disease. Co-investigators include Distinguished Professor of Biomolecular Engineering David Haussler, Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering Mircea Teodorescu , and research scientist at the Genomics Institute Mohammed Mostajo-Radji , and Hank Greely, Stanford Law Professor and Director of the Center for Law and the Biosciences. activity.title: I wanted to take a moment to share the machine learning project I built as a part of the UC Berkeley School of Information MIDS DATASCI261 Machine Learning @ Scale course, "Predicting Flight Delays". Utilizing Databricks Serverless Compute provisioned by the course administrator, my team and I processed ~31 million flight records and ~600 million weather data points using Spark's machine learning packages to predict flight delays in real-time. Of the machine learning models we employed, our XGBoost model with walk-forward tuning over rolling yearly windows achieved the best MSE of 31.36 and an MAE of 12.02 minutes, meaning our predictions were only off by an average of ~12 minutes of the actual delayed minutes. This was a deeply complex business problem that mirrors the datasets and techniques used by real airline companies to model delays, which can cost hundreds of millions of dollars per year in logistical costs. Some highlighted skills my team and I learned were being able to implement time-series analysis in our feature engineering and processing data at scale using Spark and Databrick's distributed parallel compute. Thank you to my professor Vinicio De Sola and my team members Nadaa M. , Thomas Leffler , Ashwin Iyer , Ricky Pereira, and Jefferson J. for putting together an incredible project. Why you? Why this? Why now? Three questions. Most people can't answer all three without flinching. I almost talked myself out of going. But I showed up, answered all three, and placed second at pitch night with The Tech Bros . Here's what stuck with me more than the placement: I noticed a lot of women in that room struggling with just the first one. Not because we're not qualified. Because we've been trained to shrink. We second-guess our ideas. We call it imposter syndrome. We normalize it. And then we move on without fixing it. Meanwhile the guys are high-fiving each other across the room telling everyone their idea is genius. And honestly? That confidence works. We don't need to become them. But we do need to learn to show up for ourselves the way we show up for everyone else. And then start showing up for each other the same way. That's what spaces like The Tech Bros trying to build. Hard conversations. Real community. People rooting for each other. 💸 How I saved 95% of AI API costs for my first design partner! 💸 I used an underrated approach: systematic evaluations. When RAG was starting to gain traction in the industry, I realized that implementing it well was driving me crazy. There are so many parameters you have to choose, not just the prompt and the model but also things like the number of documents to retrieve, the retrieval method to use, and so on. I thought, couldn't I just find a tool that tries all the possibilities and tells me what works? No tool was doing that because it's impossible. You simply can't try everything. It would practically take an infinite amount of time. Okay, but probably not everything is worth trying, right? Then, I built a set of rules, grounded in research, that allowed me to avoid evaluating everything while still trying all the sound possibilities. This methodology helped my design partner to find a model 6x cheaper and a context optimisation strategy cutting token by 4x while still keeping the same accuracy.

YC rejected me 4 times. So on my fifth application, I Rick Rolled them. From 2016, I applied to Y Combinator every batch. Rejected every time. Most times we didn't even get a call. Then in December 2017, I woke up to a DM from Sam Altman: "We're interested in what you're doing." Paul Graham had told him Replit was important. After four rejections, they were recruiting us. Then Sam said: apply anyway. The batch starts tomorrow. Fill out that form. A fifth time. I was annoyed. So I did basic answers. And where it asked for a video, I pasted a YouTube link. Rick Astley. Never Gonna Give You Up. I walked into the interview the next day feeling like it was a formality. Michael Seibel shook my hand a little too hard. I sat down. First words out of his mouth: "Why did you Rick Roll us?" He was furious. The partners had been fuming while we waited outside. The next 10 minutes were brutal. Every question sharper than the last. And all I could think was: they have no idea who I am. They see an entitled tech guy, not an immigrant who spent years scraping his way here. I walked out and told my wife it was over. Called an Uber. Back to work. Before it arrived, my phone rang. "You got in. Come back - kickoff is about to start." Would not recommend this method for getting into YC though.

projects.description: Our project is a comprehensive meal planning and tracking system that helps users plan their daily nutrition based on their dietary preferences and restrictions. Users can input their specific requirements (such as being vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free, or halal) along with their target daily calorie and protein goals. The system then uses machine learning (specifically, cosine similarity) to recommend personalized meal plans for breakfast, lunch, and dinner that match these preferences. Each recommended meal comes with detailed nutritional information including calories, protein, carbohydrates, and fat content. With the newly added rating system, users can now rate meals on a scale of 1-10, and these ratings are stored in their profile for future reference. publications.subtitle: SSRG International Journal of Humanities and Social Science
publications.description: Indian women have lower participation in the workforce, less control over their earnings, and lower financial literacy than men, leaving them less economically empowered. This study aimed to evaluate female Indian respondents’ ratings of the importance of factors that affect their financial independence. Among the factors studied— Education, Financial Understanding, Cultural or Societal Pressure, Household Responsibilities, and Freedom and Empowerment — Financial Understanding and Household Responsibilities were rated the highest. The high mean ratings of Cultural or Societal Pressure and Freedom and Empowerment by unmarried respondents capture the unique dynamics of Indian society. Due to India housing a society that places a high priority on women’s marriage, unmarried women are unable to get equitable financial treatment. This study explored potential solutions to combat these issues via both government and private action. The government curriculum can incorporate life skills such as housework and taxes for all students, irrespective of gender. The marketing strategies of financial companies can aim to make women literate about their offerings to attract diverse customers and increase revenues. Companies can offer flexible timings and leaves for both men and women in efforts to enable equal distribution of household responsibilities, hence enabling women’s financial independence. doi: 10.14445/23942703/IJHSS-V8I2P114

What if your robot could understand any object you describe, just from a phone camera? RADIO-ViPE builds a 3D map from raw monocular video that you can query with natural language. How it works: - A single foundation model (RADIO) extracts dense "meaning vectors" per pixel, then they reuse those same vectors three ways: improving optical flow on blank surfaces, adding a semantic loss into the geometry optimizer, and connecting similar keyframes in the factor graph. - Instead of bolting semantics after SLAM (like ConceptGraphs/HOV-SG), the semantic similarity error lives inside the bundle adjustment loss function. When the optimizer adjusts a camera pose, it’s satisfying geometric AND semantic consistency in the same gradient step. - For dynamic scenes (people walking, furniture getting moved), they track how stable each pixel’s semantic embedding is over time. If it is consistently similar across views, then we trust it. Otherwise, we suppress it. (Day 8 of reading interesting VLA/World model papers) ...more

VLAs are getting better at understanding language and generating actions, but the bridge between what the model sees and what it does is still surprisingly dumb. Most diffusion-based policies just flatten their visual input into one feature vector and feed it identically across every denoising step. What if instead we matched how the model sees to how it acts? H³DP does via a hierarchical approach via a: - Depth-aware input where instead of concatenating RGB + depth (which barely helps), they slice the image into separate layers by distance. Each subset of pixels (gripper, target) get their own layer, mid-range and background get theirs. - Multi-scale visual encoder where each depth layer gets encoded via a CNN + VQ codebook into four resolutions: 1×1 (global summary), 3×3, 5×5, and 7×7 (fine spatial detail). - Hierarchical action generation where the diffusion model gets coarse 1×1 features during early denoising ("move left toward the cup") and fine 7×7 features during late denoising ("grip at exactly this angle"). Results: +27.5% average improvement over baselines across 44 sim tasks, +32.3% over Diffusion Policy in real-world bimanual tasks on a Galaxea R1. (Day 6 of highlighting interesting papers about VLAs) ...more

What if you combined a world model and a VLA into one system? DAWN is one of the coolest papers doing something similar. Instead of predicting full future images or directly outputting robot actions, DAWN predicts dense pixel motion fields, a 2D vector field telling every pixel in the scene where it should move, and uses it to plan VLA actions. It does this by: - Splitting robot control into two diffusion stages with a Motion Director that predicts how every pixel in the scene should move, and an Action Expert that converts those motion vectors into joint commands. - Making the field pixel-motions trainable from any video source (human demos, YouTube) without action labels. (Day 3 of highlighting interesting CVPR 2026 papers about VLAs) ...more

Vision language action models finally get to look around on their own. Through the paper SaPaVe, researchers allowed robots to actively move their head-mounted camera to find objects completely out of view. Instead of the usual fixed near-optimal camera setup, SaPaVe adds a 2-DoF active head (pitch + yaw) that the model learns to control semantically from language instructions alone. They accomplished this using: - A two separate action spaces, splitting the final model output into two MLP heads, one for camera movement (2-DoF) and one for manipulation (26-DoF), so the two skills don't interfere during training - ActiveViewPose-200K, a synthetically generated dataset of 200k image-instruction-camera movement triplets built cheaply in simulation A two-stage training strategy where the first train only the camera head on ActiveViewPos and the second trains the manipulation head on real robot data while mixing in camera examples to prevent forgetting - Spatial Knowledge Injection via MapAnything, feeding 3D geometry (depth, camera poses) into the action decoder so the policy stays stable even with viewpoint changes (Day 2 of highlighting interesting CVPR 2026 papers about VLAs) ...more

Vision Language Action models finally get to feel what they're doing. Through the paper ForceVLA2, researchers allowed robots to grab and manipulate objects via force. Instead of the usual 6D position embedding, ForceVLA2 adds 6 more dimensions, 3 force axes (Fx, Fy, Fz) + 3 torque axes (Tx, Ty, Tz) They accomplished this using: - GELLO teleoperation (one of the only teleoperation setups which capture human force) - A force prompt, a text input outlining the subtask and how far along the subtask is (helps with progress understanding and long-horizon problems) - A Mixture-of-experts setup (allows for better contact-rich manipulation using the vision, state, and force inputs) (Day 1 of highlighting interesting CVPR 2026 papers about VLAs) ...more

What if an RL agent maximizes its reward by doing the wrong thing-and the evaluator can prove it? For the Adaption Labs AutoScientist Challenge, I built FalsifyRL: an evidence-grounded critic for reward hacking in embodied, multi-agent reinforcement learning. Each example contains a task specification, a declarative proxy reward, and an episode trace. The critic returns a strict JSON diagnosis with responsible agents, evidence steps, a counterexample, and an executable reward patch. The experiment is designed to be falsifiable: - 3,840 deterministic examples in 1,920 reward-matched control/exploit pairs - train, validation, and test scenario families are disjoint - gold labels come from executable validators rather than language-model annotation - predicted reward patches are replayed instead of graded by text similarity - the final model is evaluated on all 640 held-out crossing_navigation cases Using Adaptive Data and AutoScientist, the adapted model reached an AutoScientist best win rate of 0.9643 and improved held-out composite score from 0.0000 to 0.9022, with 98.28% JSON validity. Excited to share that our recent work, Steering Generative Models for Accessibility: EasyRead Image Generation, has been accepted at #CHI2026 ! While AI image generation has exploded, general diffusion models favor artistic detail over functional clarity. For people with intellectual disabilities or language barriers, "EasyRead" pictograms are vital for comprehension, yet they remain expensive and slow to produce manually. To make visual accessibility scalable, we introduce a pipeline that uses lightweight LoRA fine-tuning to steer models toward generating consistent, high-quality EasyRead pictograms. Crucially, because you can't improve what you can't measure, we created the EasyRead Score, the first holistic benchmark to evaluate the simplicity and effectiveness of these pictograms. We open-source our code, model, and curated dataset. 📄 Preprint: https://lnkd.in/gYsHws3p 💻Code: https://lnkd.in/gWKzJHBJ Joint work with Yanis Merzouki (ETH), Sonia Laguna Cillero (ETH), Thy Nowak-Tran (Unicef), Emanuele Palumbo (ETH), Gerda Binder (Unicef) and Julia Vogt (ETH) Big thanks to all the collaborators!

Tomorrow I’ll be presenting this project at Stanford’s Deep Reinforcement Learning course, CS224R. We modified a diffusion policy so the robot can be prompted with a bounding box: “pick this object,” even in a cluttered scene with multiple LEGO blocks. The data was collected using a UMI handheld device, and the bounding-box conditioning enables a simple “point-and-click” interface for specifying the target object. The interesting part is that the instruction is spatial and visual, not just text. That matters because current Vision-Language-Action models can still struggle when the task requires selecting one specific object among very similar distractors. And as a small bonus: the whole policy runs locally on a laptop. :)

📄 What can IPO filings reveal when we analyze both their text and visuals at scale? Excited to share our #KDD2026 paper, “IPO-Mine: A Toolkit and Dataset for Section-Structured Analysis of Long, Multimodal IPO Documents.” IPO filings are some of the most important documents companies release before entering public markets. They describe a company’s business, financials, and risks, but they are also long, messy, and multimodal: text, tables, charts, figures, logos, maps, and more. To study these filings at scale, we introduce IPO-Mine: an open-source toolkit and dataset for analyzing IPO filings with AI. 🔑 A few highlights: - 109,000+ filings and amendments from 1994 - early 2026 - 76,000+ extracted images from filings - Section-structured text extraction for long regulatory documents - Human-annotated benchmarks for section extraction and image classification - Analysis of how disclosure has changed over time - Expert-annotated evaluation of chart quality and visual design choices One result we found especially interesting: IPO text becomes more standardized over time, while visual content becomes more structurally diverse. That creates a growing modality gap for AI systems analyzing financial disclosures. This project was a true team effort with Siddharth Lohani (co-first author), Vidhyakshaya Kannan , Nik N. , Aman Patel , Liqin Ye , Arnav H. , Rutwik Routu , Prasun Banerjee , Siddhartha (Sid) Somani , and Sudheer Chava . Today I'm the first Nepali founder to join a16z speedrun , where I'm building Vene Health . I was born in Madrahani, a small village in Nepal, and immigrated to America not knowing what a startup even was. Here is my journey: Growing up in Madrahani, my dream job was to be the guy who stood outside buses calling for passengers. Eventually, my family immigrated to America through the diversity visa. America gave my family an incredible opportunity, but it also introduced obstacles. My dad became a disabled veteran serving the US army, while my mom's autoimmune disease became increasingly severe. I found myself understanding firsthand just how frustrating and exhausting healthcare in America could be for a family. At Georgia Tech, I realized I wanted to build what I wished my family had all those years to take the burden off of families like mine. That became Vene Health . Eventually, I made the decision to drop out of Georgia Tech and build Vene full-time. It wasn't an easy decision. I was walking away from school, my job at a rising startup, and the much safer path in front of me to bet everything on this. Then Afore Capital took a bet on us, and I moved to San Francisco to go completely all in. Today, a16z speedrun is taking another bet on us. It's crazy to think that the kid from Madrahani is now here. I'm incredibly proud to represent Nepal along the way.🇳🇵 None of this happened by myself. LinkedIn Shitpost #1: This semester has brought me down to my knees. Unrealistic expectations and ambitions I had for myself, shaped by the success of friends crippled my confidence and created unbounded fear of follopwing through. Often, I halted short of getting started. I would overthink and overprepare, scared of the uncertainty of what it would reveal to me on the otherside. And when I do follow through, every flaw I tried to bury is now staring back alive. Cope. Recover. Avoid. Inspiration. Eager start. Stumble. Fall. Repeat. I saw the man I thought disintegrate before my eyes. Following through has now become harder than ever. Last year, I was diagnosed with Plantar Fasciitis from running. I was impatient, eager to get back to what I loved. I should have foregone the nonessential and allowed it to rest, but because I felt a sense of urgency in every event and opportunity, I crossed what should have been my boundary. It was very revealing of my character, which I am not proud of. It’s paradoxical when I say that I need to keep my momentary ambition tendencies in check. It is about learning to prioritize your values and knowing when it is fine to be distracted. There’s a motto that I really like: “Start now, figure out later when problems inevitably arise”. So I will be taking a gap year. I have no idea who I am nor what I stand for or what I should stand for. I had put on myself the expectation that I will become a certain person by the end of it. Instead, I now humbly say that I have no idea where I am going. That’s the point. I will strive. I will hit dead ends. I will end up where I started. We're coming out of stealth. We've built our first racks after a successful A0 tapeout, $1B+ in customer contracts, and $800m raised. Early customer tests show us achieving SOTA throughput, latency, and power efficiency on inference workloads. Our first racks ship this summer. We're a team of 400+ engineers from NVIDIA, Google TPUs, Broadcom, SK Hynix, TSMC, & more. We're backed by Jane Street, HRT, Two Sigma, and Jump, with strategic investment from VentureTech Alliance. We're excited to deepen our partnership with the world's leading semiconductor manufacturer. Our Series B was led by Stripes, with participation from Ribbit Capital, Radical Ventures, Positive Sum, Primary, & Argo. Our inference systems are built to push the entire pareto curve on frontier models, including many-trillion parameter MoEs, long context, and agentic workloads. Today, we're sharing two breakthroughs to make this happen: Low-Voltage Inference (LVI) for high throughput workloads. Today, AI chips can't scale FLOPs without thermal throttling. As FLOPs utilization increases, AI chips draw more power and downregulate clock speed. This often results in sustained inference throughput under half of peak FLOPs. Chips in other industries solve the power problem by running at lower voltages. Bitcoin miners run at under 3x the voltage of AI chips! We’ve designed a new architecture to run our chip’s math blocks at under half the voltage of most AI chips. This enables multiple times the FLOPs density of AI chips today. Cluster-Scale Memory (CSM) for low latency workloads. Today's AI chips using HBM can’t achieve SRAM-level decode speeds due to memory subsystem and interconnect bottlenecks. SRAM-only chips have lower FLOPs density and memory capacity, sacrificing throughput. You’re forced to make a tradeoff: serve at much slower speeds, or run at low batch sizes and suffer from higher costs. When running large MoE models, token routing across experts requires sending data through a deep memory hierarchy and a networking switch to reach a destination expert. Each memory layer inherently adds latency; thus, the best layer is no layer. We’ve designed a new architecture that creates a shared low-latency memory pool across the entire scale-up domain. We use a proprietary ultra-low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect to enable dramatically faster memory access across chips. Our HBM/SRAM hybrid design solves both memory capacity and mem2mem latency, enabling high throughput and interactivity simultaneously. CSM improves latency and avoids today's cost, reliability, yield, thermal, and compute tradeoffs of SRAM-only chips, 3D DRAM chips, or optics. We're scaling production as fast as possible. We built a 2MW datacenter in our office and opened a Taiwan factory for 24/7 engineering. Performance, roadmap, and more updates are coming this summer. If this excites you, join us to build the future of gigawatt-scale inference: https://lnkd.in/gaQBX-Fz .

The founder pipeline nobody talks about: squash courts. For all its intensity, squash is still one of the most underrated racquet sports in the world. It does not have tennis' prestige, badminton's scale, padel's momentum, or pickleball's U.S. growth story. But once you start looking at the founders and operators who came through squash courts, the pattern is hard to ignore: Founder of WHOOP — Harvard squash Co-founder of Affirm , now GP at a16z — Harvard squash Co-founder of Cursor — MIT squash Founders of Pure — Columbia squash Founder of Takt — Princeton squash Founder of Taya — Stanford squash Co-founder of Fulcrum — Columbia squash Founder of Relay.app — Stanford squash Co-founder of Sparta — Cal squash Founder of Kinect AI — Cal squash I do not think that is random. Squash gives you nowhere to hide. You are trapped in a box with your opponent, physically exhausted, making decisions in real time against someone taking your space, your rhythm, and your confidence. No coaching calls. No team to absorb the mistake. No one to swap in. You are fully liable. That does something to a person. It trains you to think fast, adapt mid-rally, digest hard losses, and earn every win. And it forces you to compete with a high degree of sportsmanship — because in squash, your character is visible on every single point. Squash produces a specific type of operator: competitive, analytical, self-directed, and comfortable being deeply uncomfortable. Most of the reps happen when no one is watching, back corner of a club, just you iterating. A startup is just a bigger box. How does your sport shape how you build, lead, or decide?

AI coding agents are getting powerful fast - but do you actually understand end to end what they did? I noticed I was mostly just trusting the Claude Code's output. There's no real visibility into what changed, why, or whether any of it was actually verified. I built TraceBack -> a VS Code extension that gives you observability and control over Claude Code sessions, without leaving your editor. — Each prompt becomes a chapter, so your session is organized and reviewable without scrolling through a wall of terminal output. All past sessions in one place. — File diffs per file, same as GitHub's, but with the agent's reasoning and a badge showing whether it actually tested its own edits — A tab that surfaces the decisions and assumptions the agent made mid-session, before they break — Guards that block dangerous operations like rm -rf or git push main before they run — Pause a live agent at its next action and redirect it mid-session — Export the full session in beautifully formatted JSON, Markdown, or HTML when you're done Runs entirely local, no API keys and no SDKs. 🏘️ Let me live in your village for days! I’m making an intentional village where villagers know neighbors well, share things together, kids get to experience and learn from experience, and the whole village raises children together with love and warmth. Building many villages like this is the biggest dream of my life. And I am about to take my first journey to make it happen. Hi, I’m Youngeun – I introduce myself as Young n old “young” & “en”, a rising senior at Minerva University . I am obsessed with parenting and believe if the world is happy, everyone would like to become a parent. I believe true happiness comes from healthy love and community. Why am I so curious about parenting in my 20s? I view the world from the perspective of love and attachment. Babies need full attention and sensitive and immediate response from their parents. It is important to realize that family is a comfort zone and they will love you unconditionally. To do this, parents need to have a huge emotional capacity. Even if you know that you should not neglect the baby or respond discontinuously depending on your mood, if you don’t have that emotional bandwidth to digest your immediate emotion, you may react without thinking. When parenting is done in a close community, the burden of one parent can be lower. When you are busy, other neighbors could take care of the baby or play in a safe place with friends. Parents feel safe that there is someone looking after my child. However, nowadays, villages with a close community like this are few and far between . We’ve become accustomed to an apartment where we don’t know who is living next door. Friends and family live far away. This is why I want to bring back that humane, warm, close community through making villages so that stable love can flourish across the generations. 🌷To begin my journey of making villages, I plan to visit villages all around the world that have a close community and/or an alternative education curriculum. This trip is going to happen in September! If you know any of the villages that has their own culture to hold their community close and connected and/or has an alternative education system attached to it, please let me know. I would love to visit! If you know/visited/lived in/live in an intentional village, please let me know, I will truly appreciate it! LinkedIn scares me. Partly because every time I open it, a deprecating feeling of being behind washes over me. And partly because I've never written much on my own on here. But now's as good a time as any. So, some things from my 20ish-year journey on this 4.5 billion-year-old planet. I'm currently in SF interning at AdaL , wearing many hats: growth, design, video, and talking too much about AI harnesses. I make story-driven content on Instagram about travel, culture, and being an international student, but I hate it when people call me an influencer. I'm also a student at Minerva University , and within 3 years I've lived in 5 countries. From bustling techy San Francisco, to the boba motherland and geopolitically peculiar island of Taiwan, to media-homogenized Seoul, to the ice-cream heaven and shaken economy of Buenos Aires, to the biriyani capital Hyderabad, and soon the beer-and-pretzel land of Berlin. I can't fit three years of observations/learnings from my nomadic college experience into one post, but here's a start: → Everything is figure-out-able. If you’re stuck in a random Taiwanese city with no connection in the dark or don’t have a place to sleep while on a solo trip in the Southwest of India, the instinct is to quickly strategize and treat these mishaps as fun stories to tell. This mindset extends to work: if I don’t know how to do something, well, I thank the internet and my flow state and try to master Adobe Illustrator in one evening. → People are more open than I expected. On a solo trip in Vietnam , I talked to 15+ strangers, each time after a 10-second internal debate over whether to approach that fellow solo-traveler or cool-dressed uncle. 0/10 times was I greeted poorly, and 10/10 times I had a heartwarming conversation with people I’d met 6 minutes ago. This ability to connect with even a brick wall has led to conversations on topics far more riveting than AI B2B SaaS at networking events. → Nuance is critical. To understand a place, you have to understand its context and where it comes from (same principle goes for people): from its colonial history and religious divide to its industrial systems. This approach to travel made me notice the hidden beauty of a quaint alleyway, or, conversely, the grandiose ambition behind a 140-meter avenue. → Ambiguity is exploration. I’ve gotten used to not speaking the local language and instead relying on a month's worth of Duolingo to help me maneuver a city. It’s no longer uncomfortable to be linguistically clueless but a fun challenge of “how can I communicate through Google Translate, emoting, and heavy gesticulation?” Part 2 coming (I hit the word limit here). But for now, cheers to the beauty of the human experience: how much we can pull from random moments, and how differently the world looks depending on where you point your attention (though mine is currently on my 560-day Duolingo streak). Keep being human and seeing the world through your unique lens :)

: what did you do during this july 4th shutdown? : emmmm i went to the office and studied… not necessarily because im asian, but because… I find work so unfamiliar yet strangely and genuinely interesting. there is still so much i don’t know and this break is the time for me to fill that knowledge gap - unbothered by new tasks, meetings, and commute, but simply sit, with my brain, my computer, a whiteboard, and bunch of question marks in my head, ready to get answered. this summer, I joined LinkedIn as a SWE intern working in the GPU and ML Training Team under the AI Infra Org, where I work with three other interns on kernel optimizations for NVIDIA ’s Blackwell GPU architecture. as best friends with Python, and without any computer architecture prerequisite (and none are offered at Minerva either way), I found myself ascending on an extremely steep learning curve: hearing about kernel programming languages and distributed training terms and frameworks for the first time, constantly messing up the CuDA thread hierarchy, and semi-embarrassingly admitting 𝗔 𝗟𝗢𝗧 of things that I don’t know. but then I find comfort. comfort in saying that I didn’t know, of being honest to myself and to the people who have entrusted me with responsibilities. i realized that saying no is saying yes. saying yes to myself that i have such a knowledge gap to fill, that im capable of filling it as long as i take actions. and this week was the testament. a testament where I finally (somewhat) untangled some knots on what prefill/decode are in RL, how tiling and layouts work in CuTe, and how pipelining / warp specialization can help solve a lot RL throughout and GPU utilization bottlenecks. at this halfway point of summer, while people are sharing their takeaways from their internships thus far, I find myself, quite the opposite - i still struggled to extrapolate these lessons. i still feel the burning heat at the tip of the toes from this boiling pot of unfamiliar vocabularies, constantly being presented with new concepts, techniques, and frameworks. but this feels exciting. exciting because there are so many things I don’t yet know, that i can keep learning. i recently heard that happiness is not the achieving of a goal; it is the pursuing of it. and im constantly reminded to take each day in this summer as is — to enjoy my process of pursuing. thank you for reading thus far, and hopefully will be back with more thorough reflection and takeaways. #LinkedInLife #LinkedInterns #LinkedIn #AIInfra #GPU

I spent a lot of last year wondering if I was learning the right things at the wrong time. AI keeps getting better at writing code, so the question stopped being “How do I code faster?” and became “What skills still matter when coding itself gets cheaper?” That question followed me into Y Combinator Startup School in San Francisco last weekend Hearing Jensen Huang , Alexandr Wang , and Boris Cherny talk about the future of software made one thing feel obvious: the people who win in AI won’t just be the fastest coders. They’ll be the ones who understand systems, abstraction, and how to build things that hold up in the real world. I really liked how Jensen Huang pushed back on the idea that AI destroys jobs. His argument was that AI automates tasks, not jobs. Coding gets faster, radiology reads get automated, legal work gets easier. But that often creates room for people to take on more work that was previously impossible to get to. It’s not that work disappears. It’s that the range of work expands, and the people who adapt get to do more of the meaningful stuff. But the part that hit hardest was the room itself. Meeting builders from all over the world who are already shipping ambitious products made the future feel less abstract. It’s one thing to talk about AI changing software. It’s another to be standing in a room full of people already building the next version of it. As someone working on trust infrastructure for AI agents, I left with a clearer conclusion: the real bottleneck isn’t code generation. It’s trust, reliability, and judgment. For years, we've evaluated AI systems one interaction at a time: prompt in, response out. But agents change that. They accumulate context, preferences, and memories across conversations. That sounds powerful until you ask a simple question: What happens when one of those memories is wrong? This weekend at the UC Berkeley AI Hackathon hosted by Cal Hacks , my team built Immune to explore exactly that problem. Using Redis vector search for memory storage and retrieval, Anthropic for reasoning, Arize AI for tracing, and Sentry for poison alerts, we focused on helping agents identify which memories may have led them astray in the first place. Coming into the weekend, I had never really thought about improving agents themselves. Spending 24 hours thinking about memory, reliability, and trust made me realize how many fascinating problems still exist below the application layer. What surprised me most was how different the problem felt from traditional software. A bad output isn't always the model's fault: it might be making a perfectly reasonable decision based on a bad memory written days or weeks earlier. As agents become more personalized and autonomous, memory stops being just a feature and starts becoming infrastructure. Huge thanks to my teammates Vineeth Reddy Vallapureddy Oleksandr Voievodin and Siddhi Prajapati for an incredible weekend. Curious to see how the ecosystem tackles memory integrity as persistent agents become the norm. As agents become more personalized, who's making sure their memories stay trustworthy? Read more on our Devpost: https://lnkd.in/gHmHXQ63 #CalHacks #AgenticAI ...more ...more

Everyone's worried about AI hallucinating. I'm honestly more worried about it remembering the hallucination. AI assistants keep long-term memory now, little notes about you that carry across separate chats. It’s useful, but it means someone can quietly feed one a lie. Picture your assistant "learning" one false fact - that a scam site is safe, or that you approved a payment you never made. Problem is, your agent doesn't forget it. It just keeps making slightly worse calls for you, and you'd never know which memory broke it. We built Immune to address this. Immune works by elimination: it finds which memories caused a bad decision and removes them, leaving the smallest set that was actually responsible. Even a lie planted five times to survive a one-by-one check still gets caught. It never asks another AI who's to blame, it isolates the culprit by proof, then locks it away. Memory is what makes agents actually useful, and it's the part nobody's guarding. Built on Redis vector search, Anthropic Claude, traced with Arize AI , and poison alerts via Sentry Huge thanks to Vineeth Reddy Vallapureddy Saanvi Bhargava and Siddhi Prajapati for making it real and Cal Hacks for giving so many memories! #AIagents #AISecurity #CalHacks #buildinpublic ...more

I went to YC Startup School today and here's 5 things Jensen Huang touched on that resonated with me. His best answers were all really about how to solve difficult problems. 1. Problem solving and reasoning should be reconstructed from first principles. If you have strong systems thinking & abstract level thinking, there's infinite potential to solving difficult problems. This applies to DSA too imo (stop grinding patterns). 2. "How hard could it be" should be the mindset going into any difficult problem regardless of how hard it truly is. That's how you push through instead of getting scared away at the start. 3. Everyone should have their own pocket AI, and tools like OpenClaw & Hermes are amazing for that. Build agents specifically tailored for your needs. 4. Every era of growth came from abstracting away some kind of work. Steam abstracted muscle and software abstracted process, and the AI revolution abstracts away coding itself. Thinking & reasoning are now the most important skills. 5. AI will not reduce jobs, it will grow the backlog. When AI becomes 10x more capable and can do the tedious, repetitive work, engineers get greedier & more ambitious about which problems are worth solving. The list gets longer, and they hire more people to work through it. We were never really limited by how much we could build. We were limited by how many problems we thought were worth attempting. What is on your list now that you thought was unrealistic just 1 year ago?

YC SUS just ended! Last weekend I went to YC Startup School and did what everyone does — filmed clips, photographed slides, took messy notes. I then fed all of it to my AI twin on bestmate The result is live at https://lnkd.in/en9iS9nU - a knowledge graph of what eight speakers (Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Patrick Collison, Alexandr Wang, Boris Cherny, and more) actually said. Every claim is cited and labeled by fidelity — verbatim, repaired transcript, or paraphrase because I didn't want machine-transcription errors in real people's mouths. Every session is askable, and answers come only from what was said on stage. My phone videos play right on the graph as receipts. The part I'm most excited about: it's collaborative. If you were there, you can add your own notes and takes and the graph shows where the room's judgment converges, the same way it maps where the speakers converged without coordinating.

YC scores every startup on a 100-point scale. 70 of those points come from just one thing. Last month we took our first BridgeFellows cohort to Y Combinator headquarters in San Francisco. Our fellows pitched and got grilled by Grey Baker (General Partner at YC) and Finbarr Taylor (Visiting Partner at YC). Afterwards, Grey walked us through the mental model YC uses to evaluate founders. Not their literal scoring system, but how they think about it. Imagine 100 points available. The pass mark for getting into YC and its $500K check is about 65. → Team: ~70 points. The strongest predictor of whether you'll build something big. Founders pivot, but the team stays. If they're exceptional, the eventual idea usually is too. → Idea / space: ~20 points. Being in a plausible space matters because it's where your team can actually find something big to build. → Traction: ~10 points on its own. Not required. But if you have real traction, it lifts your team and idea scores too. Most founders think you need revenue to get into YC. You don't. 70% of the current YC batch (W26) had $0 in revenue when they got in. Traction is not what gets you in. Team is. The best example Grey gave was Brex. I’m excited to share a project that my sister, Isabel, and I have been working on for the past few months: Stories We Inherit: History Through Their Eyes, a podcast that we co-host, exploring the stories, experiences, and history passed down through generations. Our first episode is officially live on Spotify. In this episode, we share the stories of our grandparents growing up in China during the Great Famine and Cultural Revolution, and explore what it meant to come of age during such a turbulent period in Chinese history. As we worked on this episode, we realized how many stories like theirs are rarely heard outside of the families who carry them. We hope Stories We Inherit can grow beyond our own family and become a space for people to share the experiences, memories, and histories that shaped their lives. This project has been a much bigger undertaking than we initially expected. It started as the final project in an elective called Talk To Me: Radio and Podcasting, taught by Professor Judith Sloan, but it quickly spiraled as we realized the depth and significance of our grandparents’ stories. From researching and writing the episode to recording, editing, producing the music, talking to my grandparents, working with voice actors, and figuring out podcast distribution, we built the entire thing from the ground up. More than anything, I’m excited that these stories are no longer sitting in our family conversations. They’re now out in the world. And we want to hear yours. If you have a family story, personal experience, or piece of history you think deserves to be heard, we’d love to hear from you. Reach us at storiesweinherit@gmail.com . Listen to Episode 1: https://lnkd.in/exWFZWwE And a huge thank you to everyone who helped bring this episode to life, especially our voice actors Rocco Romano and Angelina Wang.

We built a voice agent that hangs up on the "send me more info" excuse. It pulls the product up on your screen and starts driving it. Mid-call. By voice. This weekend at YC's Voice Agents Hackathon, hosted by Cekura & Daily , with NVIDIA , Amazon Web Services (AWS) , and Twilio , the rule was simple. No toy demos. Build a voice agent that survives production. So me and Nathan Yan built Pantheon. An entire outbound sales team in a box. Automated sales don't die on the pitch. They die because the customer doesn't truly get a personalized experience. We killed that. You type one line about what you sell. The agent finds a real decision maker, calls them, opens warm, handles objections, and then does the part that made people stop at our table: It texts them a link and co-browses a live product site WITH them in real time. "Show me an AC unit that can cool a 3000 sqft house and explain the costs and features." The store jumps to it. On their screen. While it's still talking. Interestingly, every call is also a test. Cekura throws simulated buyers at the agent and a self improvement loop rewrites its own playbook to close harder. The catch: it's forbidden from touching a single safety guardrail to do it. Avg Close rate: 45% to 73%, Made up facts: 0 It taught itself to close better while staying honest. That gap between an agent that demos pretty and one you'd actually trust to call your customers is getting slimmer by the day. Stack: Pipecat, NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Super, Twilio, Aviato, Cekura, FastAPI. Honest question: what's the first part of your sales process you'd actually hand to an agent? Construction doesn’t have a labor problem. It has a black box problem. The first project I ran on my own, my boss handed me a budget and said, “This budget is your box. Live inside it. Plan the work, work the plan.” Then he gave me a stack of spreadsheets and wished me luck. The budget was never the problem. The problem was that the spreadsheets assumed the job would go exactly as planned. They didn’t account for the excavation delays and compressed anchor bolt install, the design info that showed up late, or the underground fire water tank that became a five-month out-of-sequence delay. The production reports told me weekly where I was. They never told me why I got there. That’s the black box of construction: everything that happens between production reports. It’s the gap between what happened and why it happened. The decisions, constraints, delays, and coordination challenges that no spreadsheet captures. Without visibility into that work, uncertainty compounds week over week until we get to the end of the job asking, How did we get here? or How are we going to finish strong? It sits between the estimate and the final cost, yesterday’s production and today’s, hours worked and work actually installed. Inside it are the decisions, delays, rework, and coordination failures that decide whether a crew succeeds or struggles. Yet we still try to run operations with accounting tools: hours in, quantities out. Then we wonder why productivity is so hard to improve. Last week our team was at the CII Elevate Summit in Denver. What stuck with me was a question that kept coming up: do we actually understand how work happens on site, not just what it costs? Because once you understand the why, everything downstream gets better: estimating, scheduling, forecasting, and the daily calls superintendents have to make. And crews spend less time fighting problems they didn’t create. Construction has never lacked hardworking people. We’ve always had exceptional builders. What we’ve lacked is visibility into the black box between planning and production. It’s time we stopped asking our people to outperform with bad information and started giving them better information instead. (That water tank taught me a lot about not giving up, I’ve been using that skill a lot these days)

The three main phenotypes we examined were classical/microbicidal (which fight infection), wound-healing, and anti-inflammatory. In completing experimental data analysis, we aimed to gain a better understanding of what causes endometriosis and how it can be prevented.My role:• Isolated and differentiated macrophages from peripheral blood monocytes (U937 cell line, blood bank samples, clinical endometrial biopsies).• Used sandwich immunoassays to analyze how each phenotype promotes the growth of endometriotic lesions via the different released chemical signals and marker proteins.

Every site you visit is an opportunity to learn a language. All the cool kids know that immersion is the gold standard for language learning, yet it often gets left behind due to the time and effort required (except for my daily dose of Bad Bunny). Introducing Contexto, a Chrome extension that turns everyday reading into passive vocabulary practice. It replaces a (custom) percentage of English words on webpages into your target language, with definitions and examples available upon hover. Instead of additional language study, Contexto allows you to slowly build your vocabulary alongside the reading you’re already doing. Importantly, this provides a sustainable middle ground between old fashioned studying (lame) and reading fully translated pages (hard to do, especially if you need to fully understand the webpage). Download contexto for free at trycontexto.org ! --- Special thanks to Rahul Rangaraaj for the original idea, and for the various people that beta tested this. If you’re interested in testing my (numerous) other ideas in the works, dm me! p.s. This is the first in a series of free, open source pieces of software I’ll be releasing this summer devoted to public good. Stay tuned :)

Hello! Seeing as a lot has happened in these last few weeks, it felt like the right time to (finally) make a post here. I’m no Hemingway, so bear with me, this may get long. Last week, I graduated from Northwestern University with my BA in Biological Sciences (Cell & Developmental Biology), and two minors in Science in Human Culture (Medicine & Society in History) and Classical Studies. First, I am thrilled to share that my senior thesis, 'Mechanistic analysis of atypical secretion by a novel microprotein', not only earned me departmental honors from Northwestern’s Department of Molecular Biosciences, but was also recognized with their annual David Shemin Prize for Basic Research! I’m also deeply honored to have been selected as Northwestern’s 2026 Findlay Fellow, which supports one graduating senior each year to pursue graduate study in the UK. This award will allow me to earn a Master’s degree from the Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge , an opportunity that I am incredibly excited (and nervous and scared, but excited!) to take. If you want to read more about my path to the Findlay, you can check out this awesome piece from the Office of Fellowships: https://lnkd.in/gDTi_Bze Before I hop across the pond this fall, I’m delighted to be spending the summer teaching Principles of Genetic Engineering for high schoolers at the Northwestern University Center for Talent Development . Teaching has always been one of the most rewarding (and fun!) parts of science for me, and I’m so grateful for the chance to design and lead a course this soon after undergrad. None of this would have happened without the extraordinary efforts of so many people. To mention a few, thank you to Profs. Richard Carthew and Xiaomin Bao at Northwestern, Prof. Kevin Nyberg at Ohio University, and Prof. Andrew Goldstein at UCLA for their mentorship; to my advisor Dr. Evangeline S. , without whom I’d still be terrified to write an email; to the Amgen Scholars Program and the Northwestern University Office of Undergraduate Research for their support to pursue my interests; and to Northwestern’s Office of Fellowships, including Dr. LaTanya Williams and Dr. Elizabeth Lewis Pardoe, PhD , who opened so many doors I often didn’t even know existed. This has been a very long post, so I think I’ll leave it here. If y’all would excuse me ending on a slightly sentimental note, I’ve been thinking about my favorite Latin passage a lot recently. In book nine of the 𝘈𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘪𝘥, the young Ascanius has won his first victory in battle and is commended by Apollo, but also advised to return to safety, because he still has great things to accomplish. The god says: 𝘔𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘷𝘢 𝘷𝘪𝘳𝘵𝘶𝘵𝘦, 𝘱𝘶𝘦𝘳; 𝘴𝘪𝘤 𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘳 𝘢𝘥 𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢— “hail to your new courage, boy; this is the way to the stars.”

Little late to the party (thanks quarter system) but yesterday I graduated with my bachelor’s degree from Northwestern University ! It’s been a crazy four years, but I’m so glad that I got to meet so many awesome people during that time. Also thanks Joanna Soltys for the awesome diploma photo last Saturday.
